newsitem.title: USA: FOMC voted to keep policy tightening bias in Feb.
newsitem.headline: FOMC voted to keep policy tightening bias in Feb.

text.p: Federal Reserve policymakers voiced considerable concern at their February meeting about the risk of higher inflation and strongly backed retention of a policy bias toward tighter credit, minutes of their meeting published on Thursday showed.
At their closed meeting on Feb 4-5, members of the central bank's policymaking Federal Open Market Committee also alluded to the possibility of a setback in the then high-flying stock market.
Several members even voiced concern that an interest-rate rise at that time could have had "exaggerated repercussions" on financial markets because such a move was not generally anticipated.

In the event, the Fed raised short-term interest rates by a quarter percentage point this week after another policy-setting meeting on March 25. Tuesday's action came after Fed Chairman Alan Greenspan had set the stage for an increase in repeated rounds of Congressional testimony.
Minutes of this week's meeting will not be released until late May.
At their February meeting, FOMC members agreed that "it would be desirable to tighten before any sign of actual higher inflation were to become evident," according to the minutes.
"All the members favored or could support a proposal to maintain an unchanged policy stance," the minutes said. "The members also strongly supported the retention of a bias toward restraint."
While the FOMC did not expect a sudden surge in inflation, many members "expressed concern about the possibility of a gradual upcreep in coming quarters that might become more considerable later."
With the economy already operating at a high level, the FOMC members saw a clear risk of higher inflation stemming from potentially faster growth in labor costs.
Looking ahead, the policymakers generally expected the economy to grow at or a bit above its long-term potential, the minutes showed.
"Many observed, however, that the risks to such an outlook appeared to be tilted to the upside," the minutes said.

"The strength of the expansion in the fourth quarter, and in fact over 1996 as a whole, had heightened concerns that the economy had considerable forward momentum at a time when it was already operating at a level, especially with regard to labor resources, that could tend to generate rising inflationary pressures," the minutes added.

At least some FOMC members were even worried that economic growth in line with potential could pose a risk of higher inflation, arguing that the special factors that had dampened price pressures could dissipate.
Such special factors would include worker worry about the risk of job loss, which has helped hold down wage demands.

The FOMC concluded that consumer spending was likely to provide "important support" for sustained economic expansion. However, it alluded to a number of factors that might hold back consumer outlays including the high level of consumer debt "and the possibility of a setback in the stock market."
FOMC members also saw federal government budget policy and foreign trade acting as a drag on the economy.

"Although fiscal policy negotiations were likely to be difficult and their outcome was uncertain, members felt that there was some basis for anticipating the enactment of further legislation this year to help bring the federal budget into eventual balance," the minutes said.

The FOMC said the large increase in exports in the fourth quarter clearly was temporary, noting "some members reported that business contacts had already communicated concerns about increased competitive pressures from imports because of the rise in the foreign exchange value of the dollar," the minutes said.
